Consonantal i

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

therefore adverb

also so, and so, thus, consequently, hence, accordingly, then (drawing a conclusion)

classical

Cic. Att. 15.16a.1: itaque mē referunt pedēs in Tusculānum
Sen. Ep. 55.11: itaque mēcum studē, mēcum cēnā, mēcum ambulā

itaque

adverb, first in its clause

and so, therefore

“And so”: what follows from the facts just told. It stands first in its clause; later in the sentence only from Livy on (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • hoc igitur habēbis, novī nihil. quid ergō opus erat epistulā?

    so there you have it: no news. Then why write at all?Cic. Att. 12.1.2

  • itaque mē referunt pedēs in Tusculānum

    and so my feet are carrying me back to TusculumCic. Att. 15.16a.1

  • Sequere mē hāc ergō. — Sequor.

    Follow me this way, then. — I’m coming.Plaut. Rud. 184b–184c

Other words

  • igitur — so, then, therefore (drawing a conclusion)

    adverb, usually second in its clause · classical · Cic. Att. 13.42.3: diem meum scīs esse III Nōnās Jānuāriās; aderis igitur; Traupman 393: therefore, ergō, igitur

    “So, then”: a conclusion drawn, or a return to the point (sīc igitur vīvitur, so this is how we live: Cic. Fam. 9.26.3). In classical prose it usually follows the first word (Lewis & Short).

  • ergō — then, so (above all in questions and requests)

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Rud. 184b: Sequere mē hāc ergō.; Cic. Att. 12.1.2: quid ergō opus erat epistulā?; Traupman 393

    The “then” of talk: quid ergō?, what then?; venī ergō mēcum, come with me, then (Phaedr. 3.7.15).

  • quārē (quā rē) — and so, for this reason (leading to a request or advice)

    adverb (relative connection) · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 1.10.1: quā rē fac ut quam prīmum veniās; Quint. 1.4.12: quārē discat puer, quid in litterīs proprium, quid commūne

    “For which reason”: in Cicero’s letters it leads into the request, quā rē velim …; the Perseus text of the letters prints it as two words.

See also thus, due to, however.

SourcesLewis & Short: itaque · Lewis & Short: igitur · Lewis & Short: ergo · Lewis & Short: quare

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 393.
